Crystallographic Insights into the Structural Heterogeneities
of 2D Ruddlesden-Popper Perovskite Films
Fei Zheng, Sergey Rubanov, Christopher Hall, Jingying Liu, Mei Gao, Trevor A. Smith,
Dechan Angmo, and Kenneth P. Ghiggino*
2D Ruddlesden-Popper phase perovskites (RPPs) oﬀer signiﬁcant potential for
next-generation photovoltaics owing to their excellent intrinsic stability. Fully
understanding the crystalline conﬁguration of 2D perovskite ﬁlms is essential
for further enhancing the power-conversion-eﬃciency (PCE) of 2D perovskite
solar cells (2D-PSCs). Herein, the structural heterogeneities, including the
proﬁles of crystal orientation and defect distribution, at both the microscopic
and mesoscopic scales for 2D perovskite ﬁlms are investigated. Empty voids
are observed in the buried interface of 2D perovskite ﬁlms associated with
Brownian tree-shaped dendritic structures, and the crystal orientations of 2D
RPPs in the upper and lower parts of these areas are mismatched. This
conﬁguration hinders charge carrier transport along the vertical direction and
is likely responsible for the lower PCE of 2D-PSCs compared to their 3D
counterparts. The formation mechanism of these voids and the crystalline
mismatching are revealed based on compositional and structural analysis.
The results suggest that synchronizing the rate of crystallization in diﬀerent
ﬁlm areas may eliminate these voids and thereby reduce the PCE gap between
2D- and 3D-PSCs. This work provides a comprehensive understanding of the
crystallographic heterogeneities of 2D perovskite ﬁlms, highlighting new
pathways to design more eﬃcient 2D-PSCs based on 2D RPP ﬁlms.

ﬁnely tuned to facilitate the vertical transport of charge carriers
by forming either sequentially or sandwich-like arranged energy
band diagrams.[14,23–25] By contrast, the lateral heterogeneities of
composition and crystallinity on the macro-scale are seldom in-
vestigated, leaving many unanswered questions about their for-
mation mechanism and the correlation with device performance.
Recently, we have determined that the appearance of Brownian
tree-shaped dendrites in 2D perovskite ﬁlms generally favors sub-
stantially improved PCE values.[26] Although the formation of
these Brownian trees is accompanied by improved crystallinity
and reﬁned crystal orientation, the interior crystallographic con-
ﬁguration of these Brownian trees and their direct correlation to
the charge carrier dynamics remains to be revealed. Further im-
proving the PCE and stability of 2D PSCs relies on the thorough
investigation and modiﬁcation of the lateral heterogeneities of
2D perovskite ﬁlms.[22,27]
Visualizing the crystal orientation of 2D RPPs within the inte-
rior or speciﬁc perovskite grains of 2D perovskite ﬁlms is essen-
tial to fully understand the assembly principles of 2D perovskites
that relate to the PCE performance of 2D-PSCs. Scanning trans-
mission electron microscopy (STEM) is a powerful technique
to probe the micro-crystallinity and compositional information
of thin-ﬁlm samples through phase-contrast images and elec-
tron diﬀraction patterns (EDPs).[28,29] Loi et al. utilized the se-
lected area electron diﬀraction (SAED) method to visualize the
phase distribution of PEA2MAn−1PbnI3n+1 (<n> = 3) quasi-2D
perovskite ﬁlms along the out-of-plane direction based on distin-
guishing the EDPs of 3D-like perovskite and the n = 1 2D RPP
phases.[30] Recently, the electron-beam induced dynamic evolu-
tion of the f-PEA2PbI4 (n = 1) capping layer formed on the surface
of 3D MAPbI3 ﬁlm was tracked by STEM and nanobeam electron
diﬀraction.[31] However, until now, investigation of the lateral het-
erogeneities of 2D or 3D perovskite ﬁlms by STEM has not been
reported. In addition, the crystallization proﬁles of neighboring
perovskite grains and their contribution to the carrier dynam-
ics at grain boundaries are important to the fundamental under-
standing of 2D perovskites. To fully reveal the origin of the PCE
diﬀerence between 2D and 3D PSCs, it is essential to investigate
the assembly conﬁguration of 2D RPPs ﬁlms by means of STEM
and other microscopic probe techniques.
In this work, the microscopic heterogeneities and crystal ori-
entation proﬁles of 2D perovskite ﬁlms for 2D-PSCs were investi-
gated by SEM, STEM, and laser-induced photo-current mapping
techniques. It is shown for the ﬁrst time that the bottom sides
(buried interface) of 2D perovskite ﬁlms are occupied by a large
number of empty voids that are gathered beneath the Brown-
ian tree-shaped dendrite structures (Brownian trees), coincident
with the lateral phase distribution pattern of ﬁlms. The forma-
tion mechanism of these microscopic structural defects and their
correlation with the opto-electrical heterogeneity of 2D perovskite
ﬁlms were elucidated based on spatially resolved crystallographic
and photophysical investigations. It is proposed that fast crystal-
lization of the large-n 2D phases on the top part of Brownian trees
traps solvent on the bottom part during ﬁlm preparation, lead-
ing to the formation and accumulation of empty voids in these
regions. The detrimental inﬂuence of the empty voids and the
crystalline mismatching-induced intra-grain boundaries on the
transport of charge carriers was conﬁrmed by photo-current map-
ping. We propose that eliminating these empty voids by coordi-
nating the crystallization rate of the small-n and large-n phases
or mitigating fast phase segregation during ﬁlm formation would
improve charge carrier mobility in the vertical direction, thus im-
proving the PCE of 2D PSCs. The results reported herein enrich
our understanding of the assembly conﬁguration and lateral het-
erogeneities of 2D perovskite ﬁlms, which should prove of con-
siderable value for improved PCE and stability of 2D-PSCs and
other opto-electronic devices.

The
butylammonium
(BA)-based
2D

ﬁlm,
BA2MAn−1PbnI3n+1 (<n> = 5), prepared by hot-casting was
used in this study owing to its considerably high device perfor-
mance and the well-established crystallographic parameters of
the RPP single crystals. Our previous studies have demonstrated
that 2D-PSCs based on these ﬁlms achieved a power conversion
eﬃciency (PCE) of ≈14.5%,[17,32] which is amongst the highest
performance reported for BA-based 2D-PSCs. As indicated by
the UV–vis absorption spectrum (Figure 1a), these ﬁlms are a
phase mixture of 2D RPPs with small-n (n = 2, 3, 4, …) and
large-n (n = L). The photoluminescence (PL) spectra of the
quasi-2D ﬁlms collected from the top (ﬁlm/air) side and bottom
(ﬁlm/substrate) side are shown in Figure 1a. Both spectra fea-
ture a dominant PL peak at ≈750 nm assigned to the large-n
component, indicating the existence of exciton funneling from
small-n to large-n RPPs upon photoexcitation that quenches the
luminescence from small-n RPPs.[33] The phase distribution
proﬁle of the 2D perovskite ﬁlm along the vertical direction
can be investigated by transient absorption (TA) measurements
conducted using the top-side and bottom-side excitation modes.
As shown in Figure 1b, TA spectra collected at the initial time-
delay stage contain speciﬁc ground-state bleaching (GB) peaks
assigned to various RPP components.[34] The larger intensity
ratio of GB peaks of small-n (n = 3, 4, 5) RPPs observed with
the bottom-side excitation mode and the dominant GB peaks of
large-n (n = L) RPPs for the top-side excitation mode suggest
that the bottom part of the quasi-2D perovskite ﬁlm is occupied
by small-n RPPs, mostly the n = 3 phase, while the top part of
the ﬁlm is dominated by the large-n RPPs.
The overall crystalline conﬁguration of this 2D ﬁlm was evalu-
ated by grazing incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GI-WAXS)
conducted from the top surface utilizing a synchrotron-generated
X-ray beam with an incident angle of 0.4°. As shown in Figure 1c,
the GI-WAXS pattern features discrete Bragg diﬀraction spots
rather than Debye-Scherrer rings, suggesting the ﬁlm is highly
textured.[35] The appearance of (1̄ 1 1) and (2 0 2) diﬀraction spots
along the out-of-plane direction imply that all 2D RPP slabs are
vertically oriented relative to the horizontal substrate, which is
crucial for eﬃcient vertical charge transport to enable higher ef-
ﬁciency devices suitable for photovoltaic applications.[36] A closer
analysis of the diﬀraction spots is conducted by plotting the in-
tensity proﬁles along the horizontal direction at qz = 1.0 Å−1. As
depicted in Figure 1d, the prominent diﬀraction peak appears at
qxy = 0.84 Å−1 can be assigned to the (1 7 1) plane of the verti-
cally oriented n = 3 RPP slabs,[32] further suggesting most of the
small-n components composing the <n> = 5 quasi-2D ﬁlms is
n = 3 phase.

of the 2D perovskite ﬁlms featuring the Brownian trees, spa-
tially resolved cross-sectional characterizations were performed

on a copper grid (Figure S4, Supporting Information). The sam-
ple was immediately transferred from the SEM chamber to the
STEM column within 3 min to avoid damage caused by the am-
bient air. It was placed into the path of the electron beam and
tilted to the horizontal orientation, with the cross-section of 2D
perovskite ﬁlms normal to the “optical axis”. As illustrated in
Figure 3a, high-angle annular dark-ﬁeld (HAADF) STEM images
were obtained by collecting the scattered electrons from an annu-
lus, providing Z-contrast phase imaging scaling with the average
atomic number (Z) of the specimen.[37,38] Based on the STEM
raster scanning system, nano-beam electron diﬀraction (NBED)
with parallel illumination (< 0.3 mrad) and beam diameter of
5 nm was performed to obtain the 2D electron diﬀraction images
of the lamella in a 2D array.

2D perovskite ﬁlm areas oﬀand on the Brownian trees are shown
in Figure 3b,c, respectively. The layered distribution of Pt, Car-
bon, 2D perovskite, ITO, and Glass from up to down is apparent

material. Perovskite grains with lateral size of 1–2 μm are sepa-
rated by grain boundaries as labeled in the ﬁgure. The bending of
the top surface of the 2D perovskite ﬁlm layer in Figure 3b is as-
signed to sunken pits existing in the non-Brownian tree ﬁlm area.

(Figure 2f).

tity of empty voids that appear in the buried interface of the un-
